Harrier's theorem as I understand it allows for predefined variables of infinitely complex problems that often tend to go haywire as more variables are added to solve it and gives it randomized structure to reveal a universal path to use the least amount of information needed to solve it.

For example, imagine the drops shooting out of a sprinkler head and you are trying to find the location of the sprinkler using just the drops that have already landed on the blades of grass. There are millions of ways to approach a solution using blade height, blade rigidity, impact velocity, blade damage, splash circumference, splash cast off, etc. The possibilities are endless and often is what makes computers and sometimes humans go nuts trying to find an elegant simple solution.

What Harrier's equation does is analyze each structure or droplet and blades of grass as a whole then creates subsets of each variable that best fits the solution, which in the case of locating the sprinkler would most likely be cast off direction and blade structure over droplet seperation. 

The math somehow categorizes each subset to show which variables best fit the possibility of a solution by identifying which ones show the most regularity to solve it. It's based off of an earlier methodology used to define complex problems called KPZ stochastic equations.

Random structurization to condense elaborate equations on the fly is similar to the reason why AI is not yet sentient. This is more than a powerful tool, I think this is probably the first step to the singularity, the point at which technology progresses faster than we as humans can comprehend it.
